factual_claims.claim: Mountain Mahogany (Cercocarpus spp.) is toxic to cats
Severity grading is 'toxic' (life-threatening); per-symptom grades range moderate to fatal
Toxic principle is cyanogenic glycosides, specifically prunasin
Prunasin is hydrolyzed by beta-glucosidase to release hydrogen cyanide (HCN), which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase and halts cellular respiration/oxygen utilization
Wilted or dried leaves are more dangerous than fresh leaves due to accelerated cyanogenic conversion/release
A seed swallowed whole without chewing may not release the toxin, whereas chewing it is a serious hazard
Leaves are a toxic part
Seeds are a toxic part
Respiratory distress (panting, gasping, labored breathing) — onset within minutes to hours
Unusually bright red/pink gums and mucous membranes (blood remains oxygenated while tissues cannot extract O2)
Dilated pupils
Excessive drooling (hypersalivation)
Shock, seizures, loss of consciousness, and coma; can progress rapidly to death

claim_verdicts.claim: [isToxic] Mountain Mahogany (Cercocarpus spp.) is toxic to cats
claim_verdicts.note: Cercocarpus is a genuine cyanogenic plant (confirmed for livestock by TAMU Rangeland and Colorado State CVMBS), so it is plausibly toxic if ingested by any mammal. BUT no cat-specific authority lists it: it is NOT in the ASPCA toxic-plant list for cats, NOT on Pet Poison Helpline, NOT on VCA. All documented toxicity is for ruminants/grazing livestock, and even there poisoning is 'seldom a problem' because animals rarely browse it. The cat-specific toxicity is an unverified extrapolation from cyanogenic chemistry, not a confirmed authoritative classification.

claim_verdicts.claim: [severity] Severity is 'toxic' (life-threatening); per-symptom grades moderate to fatal
claim_verdicts.note: Acute cyanide poisoning IS life-threatening per Merck Vet Manual when a toxic dose is consumed. However for Cercocarpus specifically, authoritative range/vet sources state toxin levels are 'usually below the dangerous level' and poisoning is 'seldom a problem.' No cat-specific severity grading exists in any authority. Grading it flatly 'toxic/life-threatening' for cats overstates the documented real-world risk and is not authoritatively supported.
claim_verdicts.authority: TAMU Rangeland Plants; Merck Vet Manual

claim_verdicts.claim: [compound] Toxic principle is cyanogenic glycosides, specifically prunasin
claim_verdicts.note: The general claim (cyanogenic glycosides) is CONFIRMED by Colorado State CVMBS and TAMU Rangeland. The SPECIFIC compound 'prunasin' is NOT supported by any source for Cercocarpus; prunasin is documented in Prunus/bitter almonds, not this genus. Naming prunasin as the specific principle is an unverified/fabricated specificity, so the compound claim as written is refuted.
claim_verdicts.authority: TAMU Rangeland Plants; Frontiers/PMC cyanogenic glycoside reviews

claim_verdicts.claim: [mechanism] Prunasin hydrolyzed by beta-glucosidase to HCN, which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase and halts cellular respiration
claim_verdicts.note: The cyanide mechanism is correct: cyanogenic glycosides are enzymatically hydrolyzed releasing HCN; CN- binds ferric heme of mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, blocking the electron transport chain and arresting aerobic metabolism (histotoxic anoxia). Merck Vet Manual confirms this exactly. (The 'prunasin' label specifically is unconfirmed for this plant, but the glycoside->HCN->cytochrome oxidase pathway is sound.)

claim_verdicts.claim: [mechanism] Wilted/dried leaves more dangerous than fresh due to accelerated cyanogenic release
claim_verdicts.note: TAMU Rangeland and Colorado State confirm bruising, wilting, withering, and drying increase cyanide production, and that 'wilted leaves from cutting the plant appear to be the most dangerous.' This is well-established for cyanogenic plants generally.

claim_verdicts.claim: [mechanism] Seed swallowed whole may not release toxin; chewing it is the hazard
claim_verdicts.note: Consistent with established cyanogenic-glycoside pharmacology (Merck, VCA): toxicity requires the plant material to be chewed/crushed so the glycoside contacts beta-glucosidase to release HCN; intact seeds swallowed whole release little. This is generally accepted for pitted-fruit/cyanogenic seeds, though not stated for Cercocarpus seeds specifically by name.

claim_verdicts.claim: [toxic_part] Leaves are a toxic part
claim_verdicts.note: Colorado State CVMBS and TAMU Rangeland identify the leaves as the cyanogenic plant part; 'all parts poisonous, especially if wilted or in regrowth,' with leaves carrying the documented cyanide load.

claim_verdicts.claim: [toxic_part] Seeds are a toxic part
claim_verdicts.note: Authoritative livestock/range sources describe leaves (and 'all parts') as cyanogenic but do not single out seeds for Cercocarpus. Cyanogenic seeds are well-documented in related Rosaceae (Prunus), so it is plausible, but no source specifically confirms Cercocarpus seeds as a toxic part. Defaulting to UNVERIFIABLE.

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Respiratory distress (panting, gasping, labored breathing) onset minutes to hours
claim_verdicts.note: Merck Vet Manual lists dyspnea, hyperventilation, and respiratory failure in cyanide poisoning, with signs beginning within ~15-20 minutes to a few hours. Matches the claim.

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Bright red/pink gums (blood stays oxygenated while tissues cannot extract O2)
claim_verdicts.note: Merck Vet Manual: mucous membranes are bright red at first (then bluish) because tissues cannot extract oxygen from the blood. Mechanism explanation in the claim is accurate. Note real cases also progress to cyanosis, which the entry omits.

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Dilated pupils
claim_verdicts.note: Dilated/large pupils are a recognized sign of cyanide poisoning reported in veterinary cyanide poisoning descriptions; consistent with severe systemic hypoxia. Supported by veterinary cyanide poisoning literature.
claim_verdicts.authority: Merck Veterinary Manual / veterinary cyanide literature

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Excessive drooling (hypersalivation)
claim_verdicts.note: Merck Vet Manual lists drooling/salivation (along with watery eyes, vomiting) among cyanide poisoning signs. Confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Shock, seizures, loss of consciousness, coma; rapid progression to death
claim_verdicts.note: Merck Vet Manual: seizures/convulsions, coma, respiratory failure and death, often within 30-45 minutes during severe convulsions. Matches the claim. This is generic acute cyanide toxidrome, not Cercocarpus-cat-specific, but clinically accurate.

verify.summary:
Source provenance is weak: the entire entry derives from a single NotebookLM notebook that itself admitted its sources contained no botanical detail and falsely called this a 'common houseplant/ornamental.' Cercocarpus (mountain mahogany) is in fact a wild desert/mountain shrub, never a houseplant.

WHAT HOLDS UP: Cercocarpus is a genuine cyanogenic plant (confirmed by TAMU Rangeland Plants and Colorado State CVMBS — veterinary-college authorities). The cyanide MECHANISM (claim 4), the wilted-leaf danger (5), the chew-to-release hazard (6), leaves as toxic part (7), and the entire symptom cluster (9-13: respiratory distress, bright-red gums, dilated pupils, drooling, shock/seizures/coma/death) are all CONFIRMED by the Merck Veterinary Manual as the standard acute-cyanide toxidrome.

WHY OVERALL = FAIL: (1) The COMPOUND claim is REFUTED — sources confirm 'cyanogenic glycosides' generically but the specific naming of 'prunasin' is not documented for Cercocarpus (prunasin is a Prunus/bitter-almond glycoside). Naming a specific principle that no source attributes to this genus is a fabricated specificity, and a refuted core compound claim triggers FAIL per the rules.

ADDITIONAL FLAGS (NEEDS_REVIEW-level on their own): The cat-specific isToxic claim (1) and severity grade (2) are UNVERIFIABLE — NOT listed by ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline, or VCA; all real documentation is for grazing ruminants, where authorities note toxin levels are 'usually below the dangerous level' and poisoning is 'seldom a problem' because animals rarely browse it. The flat 'toxic/life-threatening' grade overstates documented cat risk. Seeds as a toxic part (8) is also unverifiable for this genus.

NOTE on safe_toxic_disagreement = false: this is not a safe-vs-toxic inversion (the plant is genuinely cyanogenic, just absent from cat databases), so the false-alarm/dangerous-miss flag does not apply; the failure is the fabricated specific compound plus unverifiable cat-specific framing.

RECOMMENDATION: Remove the 'prunasin' specific attribution (use 'cyanogenic glycosides' only), soften severity and the cat-specific certainty, add cyanosis as a later sign, and correct the false 'houseplant/ornamental' framing.

factual_claims.claim: Cherries are toxic to cats depending on the part: pit, seed, stem, leaf, and bark are dangerous; ripe pitted flesh is not clearly toxic.
The pit, stem, leaves, and bark contain amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside.

Amygdalin is broken down in the body to produce cyanide (hydrogen cyanide), which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase / blocks cellular oxygen utilization, halting ATP production and causing cellular asphyxiation affecting heart, brain, breathing, and nervous system.
Toxic parts (EN): Pit, Seed, Leaf, Stem (plus bark mentioned in description).
zh-TW additionally lists 果實 (fruit) and 果肉 (flesh) as toxic parts — verify, as this contradicts the EN claim that ripe flesh is not toxic.
Difficulty breathing and hyperventilation (Respiratory; rapid onset, minutes to hours).
Vomiting and diarrhea (Gastrointestinal; within 30 minutes to a few hours).
Convulsions, seizures, and twitching (Neurological; rapid onset).
Coma and shock with cardiovascular collapse leading to death if untreated (rapid onset).
Cherry-red mucous membranes/gums/skin due to cyanide blocking oxygen uptake leaving venous blood oxygen-saturated (Hematological; rapid onset).
Gastrointestinal obstruction from swallowed intact hard pit (physical hazard, plus choking risk).
Top-level severity graded 'cautious'; per-symptom: breathing=fatal, vomiting/diarrhea=moderate, seizures=fatal, coma/shock=fatal, cherry-red membranes=severe, GI obstruction=severe.
Onset of cyanide symptoms is rapid (minutes to a few hours).

verify.summary: Attempted to disprove the cherries entry; the core toxicology holds up against authoritative sources. ASPCA lists Cherry (Prunus) as toxic to cats via cyanogenic glycosides in stems/leaves/seeds, with brick-red mucous membranes, dilated pupils, difficulty breathing, panting, and shock. Merck Vet Manual confirms the cyanide mechanism exactly as described: cyanide inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, arrests aerobic ATP production, causes histotoxic anoxia hitting high-O2 organs (heart/brain), produces bright-red mucous membranes (venous blood stays O2-saturated), and acts rapidly (15-20 min to a few hours) with muscle fasciculation progressing to spasms and coma. Pet Poison Helpline confirms pit/leaf/stem toxicity, flesh-vs-pit distinction context, and the GI-obstruction/choking physical hazard from swallowed pits. Amygdalin is not named on ASPCA/PPH lay pages but is the established Prunus cyanogenic glycoside and Merck confirms Prunus cyanogenic glycosides, so the compound claim stands. No safe-vs-toxic disagreement: the entry correctly treats pit/stem/leaf/bark as dangerous and ripe pitted flesh as not clearly toxic, matching authorities. CLAIM 5 IS REFUTED BY THE ACTUAL DATA, NOT BY SOURCES: the zh-TW file does NOT list 果實 or 果肉 as toxic parts; its toxicParts are ["果核","","種子","葉子","莖"] and its description states pitted ripe flesh has no clear toxicity — consistent with EN. Two data-quality bugs flagged (not toxicology errors): (a) zh-TW toxicParts contains a stray empty-string element; (b) the EN+zh-TW "Coma and Shock" symptom is mislabeled body_system "Gastrointestinal" (should be neurological/systemic). Relevant files: /Users/sweetp/Workspace/MewGuard/cat_toxin_db/data/site/firestore/en/cherries.json and /Users/sweetp/Workspace/MewGuard/cat_toxin_db/data/site/zh-TW/cherries.json (no data/site/en/cherries.json exists).

claim_verdicts.claim: 1. [isToxic] Cherries toxic depending on part: pit/seed/stem/leaf/bark dangerous; ripe pitted flesh not clearly toxic
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists Cherry as Toxic to Cats: 'Stems, leaves, seeds contain cyanide.' Pet Poison Helpline: pits/leaves/stems contain cyanide, flesh distinction implied. Flesh-not-clearly-toxic is consistent with sources (toxic principle is in pit/stem/leaf, not pulp).

claim_verdicts.claim: 2. [compound] Pit/stem/leaf/bark contain amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA names toxic principle 'cyanogenic glycosides'; Merck confirms Prunus (cherry) contain cyanogenic glycosides. Amygdalin is the well-established Prunus cyanogenic glycoside; the specific name 'amygdalin' is not printed on the ASPCA/PPH lay pages (Merck notes glycoside class without naming amygdalin), so compound CLASS is authoritatively confirmed, specific name corroborated by toxicology literature.

claim_verdicts.claim: 3. [mechanism] Amygdalin breaks down to cyanide (HCN) inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase, blocking cellular O2 use, halting ATP, cellular asphyxiation affecting heart/brain/breathing/nervous system
claim_verdicts.note: Merck: cyanide 'binds to, and inhibits, the ferric heme moiety of mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase,' blocks electron transport, arrests aerobic metabolism causing histotoxic anoxia; high-O2 organs (heart, brain) affected. Matches entry mechanism precisely.

claim_verdicts.claim: 4. [toxic_part] EN toxic parts: Pit, Seed, Leaf, Stem (+ bark in description)
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA explicitly: 'Stems, leaves, seeds contain cyanide.' Pit/seed/stem/leaf all corroborated. Bark of Prunus is also cyanogenic per toxicology literature; ASPCA page does not separately list bark but does not contradict.

claim_verdicts.claim: 5. [toxic_part] zh-TW additionally lists 果實 (fruit) and 果肉 (flesh) as toxic parts (contradicting EN flesh-safe claim)
claim_verdicts.note: Refuted by the actual data file, not by sources. zh-TW toxicParts = ['果核','','種子','葉子','莖'] (pit, EMPTY STRING, seed, leaf, stem). Neither 果實 nor 果肉 appears. The zh-TW description explicitly states 成熟、去核後的櫻桃果肉本身沒有明顯毒性 (ripe pitted flesh has no clear toxicity), fully consistent with EN. The premise of the claim is false. Data-quality bug to fix: stray empty-string element in the toxicParts array.

claim_verdicts.claim: 6. [symptom] Difficulty breathing & hyperventilation (Respiratory; rapid, minutes-hours)
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists 'difficulty breathing, panting.' Merck: initial rapid breathing progressing to dyspnea, onset 15-20 min to a few hours. Onset window confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: 7. [symptom] Vomiting and diarrhea (GI; 30 min to a few hours)
claim_verdicts.note: Pet Poison Helpline lists upset stomach and diarrhea among cyanide-poisoning signs. GI signs corroborated; precise 30-min onset not stated by authority but plausible and not contradicted.

claim_verdicts.claim: 8. [symptom] Convulsions, seizures, twitching (Neurological; rapid)
claim_verdicts.note: Merck: 'muscle fasciculation' advancing to 'generalized spasms and coma before death,' rapid onset. Confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: 9. [symptom] Coma and shock with cardiovascular collapse, death if untreated (rapid)
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists 'shock'; Merck describes coma before death, cardiac arrhythmias, survival rarely >2h after onset. Confirmed. NOTE data bug: entry mislabels this symptom's body_system as 'Gastrointestinal' (should be neurological/systemic) in both EN and zh-TW.

claim_verdicts.claim: 10. [symptom] Cherry-red mucous membranes/gums/skin from cyanide leaving venous blood O2-saturated (Hematological; rapid)
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA: 'brick red mucous membranes.' Merck: 'Mucous membranes are bright red' (can become cyanotic terminally). Mechanism (cells cannot extract O2 so venous blood stays saturated) is standard cyanide pathophysiology. Confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: 11. [symptom] GI obstruction from swallowed intact hard pit (physical hazard + choking)
claim_verdicts.note: Pet Poison Helpline: 'Cherry pits can get lodged in the digestive tract, leading to blockages in the intestines.' Confirmed as a distinct physical hazard separate from cyanide.

claim_verdicts.claim: 12. [severity] Top-level 'cautious'; per-symptom breathing=fatal, vomiting/diarrhea=moderate, seizures=fatal, coma/shock=fatal, cherry-red=severe, GI obstruction=severe
claim_verdicts.note: No authority uses this schema's grading vocabulary, but the gradings do not contradict sources: Merck describes cyanide as rapidly lethal (survival rarely >2h), supporting fatal grades for respiratory failure/seizures/coma; GI obstruction as 'severe' is reasonable. The 'cautious' top-level is defensible given pitted ripe flesh is the only non-toxic part. No over/understatement detected.

claim_verdicts.claim: 13. [mechanism] Onset of cyanide symptoms rapid (minutes to a few hours)
claim_verdicts.note: Merck: clinical signs 'within 15-20 minutes to a few hours' after exposure; survival rarely >2h after onset. Directly confirmed.

verify.summary: Core toxicity is solidly CONFIRMED: chocolate is toxic/potentially fatal to cats; active compounds are theobromine and caffeine (methylxanthines); cats metabolize them slowly causing accumulation; mechanism is adenosine-receptor antagonism, altered intracellular calcium, and phosphodiesterase inhibition — all backed by Merck Vet Manual and Pet Poison Helpline. No safe/toxic disagreement. However, the entry has two REFUTED defects and several UNVERIFIABLE specifics, so this needs review rather than a clean pass. The most serious problem is the repeated 'internal bleeding' claim in the Cardiovascular Dysfunction symptom (claims 10 and 16): no authoritative source (Merck, ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline) lists internal/GI bleeding as a sign of methylxanthine toxicosis — authorities attribute death to cardiac arrhythmias, hyperthermia, or respiratory failure. This is a fabricated, non-standard sign and should be removed. Claim 6 (the framing that a phosphodiesterase claim was added only in zh-TW and absent from EN) is REFUTED on its premise: PDE inhibition IS in the EN raw source and Merck, while the published zh-TW description does not actually contain any PDE statement. Onset framing is partly off: Merck says clinical signs 'usually occur within 6–12 hours after ingestion'; the entry's '2–12h' GI/polydipsia onset starts earlier than authorities support (UNVERIFIABLE). The '2 grams of dark chocolate' dose (claim 13) is plausible from theobromine content (cocoa ~28.5 mg/g) and the ~60 mg/kg seizure threshold but is not stated by any authoritative source for cats specifically (UNVERIFIABLE). Also note a data-integrity bug in the published EN JSON: 'Severe Neurological Overstimulation' and 'Hyperthermia' are mis-tagged with body_system 'Gastrointestinal' instead of Neurological/Systemic. Toxicity ranking by type, white chocolate having virtually no theobromine, and toxic parts (seed/powder) are all CONFIRMED. Authoritative refs: Merck Vet Manual chocolate toxicosis; Pet Poison Helpline; ASPCA Pro toxbrief (Gwaltney-Brant).

claim_verdicts.claim: 1. [isToxic] Chocolate is toxic to cats (toxic/potentially fatal)
claim_verdicts.note: Merck and Pet Poison Helpline list chocolate as toxic to cats; death can occur from arrhythmias, hyperthermia, or respiratory failure.

claim_verdicts.claim: 2. [compound] Active compounds are theobromine and caffeine (methylxanthines)
claim_verdicts.note: Both Merck and Pet Poison Helpline name methylxanthines, specifically theobromine and caffeine; theobromine 3-10x caffeine concentration.

claim_verdicts.claim: 3. [mechanism] Cats metabolize methylxanthines much more slowly than humans, allowing accumulation from small doses
claim_verdicts.note: Slow metabolism / long half-life leading to accumulation is well documented; cats are highly sensitive. Merck gives canine half-lives (theobromine 17.5h); cat-specific kinetics less precisely published but the slow-metabolism principle is supported.
claim_verdicts.authority: Pet Poison Helpline / Merck Veterinary Manual

claim_verdicts.claim: 4. [mechanism] Methylxanthines block adenosine receptors causing CNS and cardiac overstimulation
claim_verdicts.note: Merck: methylxanthines competitively inhibit cellular adenosine receptors, resulting in CNS stimulation, diuresis, and tachycardia.

claim_verdicts.claim: 5. [mechanism] Methylxanthines alter intracellular calcium in striated/cardiac muscle, enhancing contractility
claim_verdicts.note: Merck states methylxanthines increase intracellular calcium levels; enhanced muscle contractility (tremors, arrhythmias) follows.

claim_verdicts.claim: 6. [mechanism] Phosphodiesterase inhibition claim is zh-TW-only, added in translation, absent from EN
claim_verdicts.note: Premise is false. PDE inhibition is in the EN raw source AND is confirmed by Merck (methylxanthines inhibit phosphodiesterase, elevate cAMP). Conversely, the published zh-TW description contains NO phosphodiesterase statement. So it is neither zh-TW-only nor absent from EN.

claim_verdicts.claim: 7. [symptom] GI upset (vomiting/diarrhea) onset 2-12h; high fat may trigger secondary pancreatitis
claim_verdicts.note: Vomiting/diarrhea confirmed as early signs; secondary pancreatitis from high fat is recognized in veterinary literature. Onset earliest bound (2h) is slightly earlier than Merck's '6-12h' framing for clinical signs but vomiting can begin early.
claim_verdicts.authority: Pet Poison Helpline / Merck Veterinary Manual

claim_verdicts.claim: 8. [symptom] Polydipsia/polyuria (diuretic effect) -> dehydration, onset 2-12h
claim_verdicts.note: Merck explicitly lists diuresis and increased thirst as signs; diuretic effect of methylxanthines is established. Onset window plausible though Merck frames signs at 6-12h.

claim_verdicts.claim: 9. [symptom] Severe neuro overstimulation: agitation, tremors, grand mal seizures, coma; onset 6-12h; fatal
claim_verdicts.note: Hyperactivity, tremors, and seizures are documented by Merck; signs usually within 6-12h. 'Coma' and fatal grading are consistent with severe toxicosis. NOTE data bug: published EN JSON mis-tags this symptom body_system as 'Gastrointestinal' instead of Neurological.

claim_verdicts.claim: 10. [symptom] Cardiovascular: rapid irregular heartbeats, INTERNAL BLEEDING, cardiac arrest; onset 6-12h; fatal
claim_verdicts.note: Tachycardia/arrhythmias and death from cardiac arrhythmia are confirmed, BUT 'internal bleeding' is NOT a recognized sign of methylxanthine toxicosis in any authoritative source (Merck, ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline). This element is fabricated/non-standard and should be removed.
claim_verdicts.authority: Merck Veterinary Manual / Pet Poison Helpline

claim_verdicts.claim: 11. [symptom] Respiratory distress with cyanosis -> respiratory failure; onset 6-12h; fatal
claim_verdicts.note: Merck explicitly states death is generally due to cardiac arrhythmias, hyperthermia, OR respiratory failure. Respiratory failure as a fatal endpoint is confirmed; cyanosis is a reasonable terminal-phase descriptor.

claim_verdicts.claim: 12. [symptom] Hyperthermia from neuromuscular overstimulation; onset 6-12h; severe
claim_verdicts.note: Merck lists hyperthermia as a cause of death; consistent with muscle tremor heat generation. NOTE data bug: published EN JSON mis-tags this symptom body_system as 'Gastrointestinal'.

claim_verdicts.claim: 13. [severity] ~2 grams of dark chocolate may cause serious harm to a cat
claim_verdicts.note: Plausible per theobromine content (dark choc ~5.3-5.6 mg/g; toxic thresholds 20 mg/kg mild, 60 mg/kg seizures) for a small cat, but no authoritative source states the '2 gram dark chocolate' figure for cats specifically. Treat as an estimate, not a sourced fact.

claim_verdicts.claim: 14. [severity] Toxicity ranking: cocoa powder > baker's > dark/semisweet > milk > white (virtually no theobromine)
claim_verdicts.note: Merck theobromine content: cocoa powder 28.5 mg/g > baker's 15.5 mg/g > dark/semisweet 5.3-5.6 mg/g > milk (lower) > white (virtually none). Ranking and white-chocolate caveat confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: 15. [toxic_part] Toxic parts: Seed and Powder (cacao seed/bean and cocoa powder)
claim_verdicts.note: Chocolate derives from Theobroma cacao seeds; cocoa powder and cocoa-bean hulls (mulch) are documented high-theobromine sources toxic to pets. Seed/Powder framing is accurate.
claim_verdicts.authority: Merck Veterinary Manual / ASPCA Pro toxbrief

claim_verdicts.claim: 16. [severity] Cardiovascular dysfunction includes 'internal bleeding' (verify)
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed NOT a standard sign. No authoritative source lists internal/hemorrhagic bleeding for chocolate/methylxanthine toxicosis. Authorities cite arrhythmias, hyperthermia, respiratory failure as fatal mechanisms. Recommend deleting 'internal bleeding' from the symptom notes.
claim_verdicts.authority: Merck Veterinary Manual / Pet Poison Helpline / ASPCA

factual_claims.claim: Cinnamon is toxic to cats in several forms (powder, sticks, essential oils, extracts).
Overall severity graded 'toxic'.
Toxic part is the bark (inner bark of Cinnamomum trees).
Cinnamaldehyde is the main flavour compound and a primary toxic concern.
Coumarin is present in high amounts in cassia/Chinese cinnamon and is a toxic concern.
Cats are especially sensitive because they lack the key liver enzymes needed to safely metabolise cinnamaldehyde and coumarin.
Cinnamon essential oils/extracts are far more concentrated than powdered spice and pose a much greater risk; a few drops of oil can equal ingesting a much larger quantity of ground spice.
Skin contact with cinnamon oil can cause systemic toxicity via dermal absorption even without visible skin damage.
Liver failure (hepatic, graded fatal) from serious organ damage with large/repeated essential-oil exposure.
Soreness, redness, or chemical burns of the skin (dermal, severe) on direct oil contact, rapid onset.
Tremors, shaking, ataxia (drunken gait), and seizures; also lethargy/depression progressing to collapse (neurological, severe).
Difficulty breathing (dyspnea) or open-mouth breathing from inhalation, higher risk with neat-oil nebulizers/ultrasonic diffusers or asthmatic cats (respiratory, severe).

verify.summary: The entry's core framing is REFUTED by the highest-priority authority. ASPCA classifies cinnamon (Cinnamomum, Lauraceae) as NON-toxic to cats, dogs, and horses — directly contradicting the entry's blanket isToxic=true and severity='toxic'. The real, authority-backed risk is narrow: cinnamon ESSENTIAL OIL/extract (not powder or sticks) is listed as hepatotoxic/toxic by Pet Poison Helpline, VCA, and the Merck Veterinary Manual. So the entry conflates a non-toxic culinary spice with a genuinely toxic concentrated oil, overstating severity for the common forms. The mechanism is partly right but mis-attributed: Merck confirms cats' glucuronyl transferase (UGT) deficiency makes them sensitive to PHENOLS in essential oils — but NO authoritative source names cinnamaldehyde or coumarin as the toxic principle, nor identifies 'the bark' as a toxic part; those claims trace only to blogs/commercial pages and are UNVERIFIABLE/fabricated as stated. The oil-exposure symptoms (liver failure, dermal irritation/burns, tremors/ataxia/seizures, dyspnea, vomiting/hypersalivation) ARE individually confirmed by Merck/PPH/VCA for essential oils, and ASPCA confirms inhaled cinnamon powder causes coughing/breathing trouble. Setting safe_toxic_disagreement=true and overall_factual=FAIL because the top authority calls the item non-toxic while the entry grades it toxic, and core compound claims (cinnamaldehyde/coumarin) are unsupported.

claim_verdicts.claim: 1. [isToxic] Cinnamon is toxic to cats in several forms (powder, sticks, essential oils, extracts).
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA explicitly lists cinnamon (Cinnamomum zeylanicum, Lauraceae) as Non-Toxic to Cats/Dogs/Horses. Only the concentrated essential OIL is authority-backed as toxic (PPH, VCA, Merck). Powder and sticks are NOT graded toxic by any authority — ASPCA notes spice exposure causes at most mild stomach upset, or irritation at large amounts. The blanket 'toxic in several forms' framing is refuted; risk is specific to oils/extracts.

claim_verdicts.claim: 2. [severity] Overall severity graded 'toxic'.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA grades the cinnamon plant/spice NON-toxic. A blanket 'toxic' overall grade overstates severity for the dominant forms (powder/sticks). A 'toxic' grade is only defensible for the essential oil specifically; as an overall entry grade it conflicts with the top authority.

claim_verdicts.claim: 3. [toxic_part] Toxic part is the bark (inner bark of Cinnamomum trees).
claim_verdicts.note: No authoritative source (ASPCA/PPH/VCA/Merck) identifies a 'toxic part'; ASPCA lists no toxic principles at all and calls the plant non-toxic. That cinnamon spice derives from inner bark is a botanical fact, but framing the bark as 'the toxic part' is not supported by any cited toxicology authority — it appears only in blog/commercial content.
claim_verdicts.authority: ASPCA Animal Poison Control (silent on toxic part)

claim_verdicts.claim: 4. [compound] Cinnamaldehyde is the main flavour compound and a primary toxic concern.
claim_verdicts.note: Cinnamaldehyde is indeed the principal flavour compound of cinnamon (general chemistry), but NO authoritative veterinary source (ASPCA/PPH/VCA/Merck) names cinnamaldehyde as the toxic principle for cats. Merck attributes essential-oil toxicity to 'phenols/phenolic compounds' generically. The specific 'primary toxic concern' attribution comes only from non-authoritative blogs.
claim_verdicts.authority: Merck Veterinary Manual (names phenols, not cinnamaldehyde)

claim_verdicts.claim: 5. [compound] Coumarin is present in high amounts in cassia/Chinese cinnamon and is a toxic concern.
claim_verdicts.note: Cassia containing more coumarin than Ceylon cinnamon is established food-science (and coumarin is hepatotoxic at high doses in humans/rodents), but NO authoritative feline-toxicology source (ASPCA/PPH/VCA/Merck) cites coumarin as the toxic concern for cats. The feline-specific coumarin claim is sourced only from blogs/commercial pages, so it cannot be confirmed as stated.
claim_verdicts.authority: No authoritative feline source confirms coumarin as the toxin

claim_verdicts.claim: 6. [mechanism] Cats are especially sensitive because they lack the key liver enzymes needed to safely metabolise cinnamaldehyde and coumarin.
claim_verdicts.note: Mechanism is correct but mis-named on the substrate. Merck confirms cats are deficient in glucuronyl transferase (UGT), making them very sensitive to phenols/phenolic compounds in essential oils; Pet Poison Helpline and VCA echo the enzyme deficiency. The general enzyme-deficiency mechanism is authority-backed. The specific naming of 'cinnamaldehyde and coumarin' as the substrates is NOT in authoritative sources (see claims 4-5), but the underlying mechanism claim itself is confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: 7. [mechanism] Cinnamon essential oils/extracts are far more concentrated than powdered spice and pose a much greater risk; a few drops of oil can equal ingesting a much larger quantity of ground spice.
claim_verdicts.note: Authorities consistently single out the concentrated essential OIL (not the spice) as the toxic form. Pet Poison Helpline and VCA list cinnamon oil among toxic essential oils and stress concentrated oils' danger, while ASPCA grades the spice non-toxic — directly supporting that oil >> powder in risk. The specific 'few drops = much more spice' equivalence is a reasonable paraphrase though not quoted verbatim by an authority.
claim_verdicts.authority: Pet Poison Helpline / VCA Animal Hospitals

claim_verdicts.claim: 8. [mechanism] Skin contact with cinnamon oil can cause systemic toxicity via dermal absorption even without visible skin damage.
claim_verdicts.note: Merck states essential oils are 'readily and rapidly absorbed through the GI tract, skin, lungs, and mucous membranes' and 'systemic absorption should be expected.' VCA/PPH confirm both ingestion and skin exposure can be toxic and that grooming compounds the risk. Systemic dermal absorption is authority-backed; the 'even without visible skin damage' qualifier is consistent with the absorption mechanism described.
claim_verdicts.authority: Merck Veterinary Manual / VCA Animal Hospitals

claim_verdicts.claim: 9. [symptom] Liver failure (hepatic, fatal) from organ damage with large/repeated essential-oil exposure.
claim_verdicts.note: Merck explicitly lists cinnamon oil among 'potentially hepatotoxic' essential oils and lists liver failure as a systemic sign; Pet Poison Helpline lists liver failure among essential-oil poisoning signs. claim_verdicts.claim: 1. [isToxic] Citrus fruits are toxic to cats.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA explicitly classifies both Orange (Citrus sinensis) and Lemon (Citrus limonia) as 'Toxic to Cats.' VCA also lists citrus oil among essential oils poisonous to cats. No safe<->toxic disagreement.

claim_verdicts.claim: 2. [severity] Overall 'toxic'; GI upset 'severe' and CNS depression 'severe'.
claim_verdicts.authority: ASPCA Animal Poison Control / Pet Poison Helpline
claim_verdicts.note: Overall 'toxic' classification is defensible. But grading GI upset AND CNS depression as 'severe' overstates typical exposure. ASPCA lists signs as 'Vomiting, diarrhea, depression; potential dermatitis' for plant/peel exposure (no severity qualifier). Severe CNS/systemic signs (tremors, ataxia, hypothermia, liver effects) are tied by Pet Poison Helpline to concentrated essential oils, not fruit-flesh ingestion, which is generally mild/self-limiting. Authorities do not support 'severe' for ordinary citrus fruit exposure.

claim_verdicts.claim: 3. [compound] Active compounds are citric acid, concentrated citrus essential oils, and D-limonene.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA names the toxic principles as 'essential oils and psoralens' - NOT citric acid. Citric acid is not cited by any authority as a toxic principle for cats; including it is a wrong-compound error. The entry also OMITS psoralens, which ASPCA does list. Essential oils / d-limonene are correct, but the compound set as stated is wrong (citric acid inserted, psoralens missing).

claim_verdicts.claim: 4. [compound] D-limonene is concentrated in citrus peel and oils.
claim_verdicts.note: D-limonene is the dominant compound in cold-pressed citrus peel oil (orange >67-97%, mandarin >70%). Confirmed by analytical chemistry sources. This is composition fact, not a vet-toxicology authority, but it is solidly established.

claim_verdicts.claim: 5. [mechanism] Citric acid and citrus oils irritate stomach, skin, and respiratory passages.
claim_verdicts.note: Citrus essential oils causing GI, dermal (redness/burns), and respiratory irritation IS supported by VCA. However the mechanism attributes irritation partly to 'citric acid,' which no authority identifies as the toxic principle. Because the named causal compound (citric acid) is wrong, the mechanism as stated is refuted; the essential-oil portion alone would have been confirmable.

claim_verdicts.claim: 6. [mechanism] In large exposures the oils affect the nervous system causing weakness/depression.
claim_verdicts.note: Cats are deficient in hepatic glucuronidation and metabolize essential oils poorly; concentrated citrus oils can cause weakness, lethargy, ataxia, tremors, CNS depression - and effects scale with concentration/dose. Mechanism (dose-dependent CNS effects from oils) is supported.

verify.summary: Core toxicity is CONFIRMED: ASPCA classifies both Orange and Lemon as 'Toxic to Cats' (toxic principles 'essential oils and psoralens'; signs 'vomiting, diarrhea, depression; potential dermatitis'), and VCA/Pet Poison Helpline confirm cats' heightened sensitivity to citrus essential oils (d-limonene) due to deficient hepatic glucuronidation. No safe<->toxic disagreement. Most symptom claims (GI, CNS depression, dermal, respiratory, drooling) and the peel-vs-flesh risk ranking and the cleaner/diffuser risk are all CONFIRMED against authorities. HOWEVER, overall_factual is FAIL on two grounds: (a) WRONG/INCOMPLETE COMPOUND (claim 3) - the entry names 'citric acid' as an active toxic compound, which NO authority supports; ASPCA's actual principles are 'essential oils and psoralens,' and the entry omits psoralens entirely. (b) MECHANISM error (claim 5) propagates the citric-acid attribution. Additionally claim 2 (severity) is REFUTED: grading GI upset AND CNS depression as 'severe' overstates typical mild/self-limiting citrus fruit exposure - authorities reserve severe systemic/neurologic signs for concentrated essential oils, not fruit-flesh ingestion. Recommended fixes: replace 'citric acid' with 'psoralens' as the second principle alongside essential oils/d-limonene; downgrade GI and CNS severity grading for ordinary fruit exposure while retaining higher severity flag for concentrated-oil/diffuser exposure.

factual_claims.claim: Citrus (Citrus spp., family Rutaceae) is toxic to cats.

Overall severity graded 'toxic'; symptom-level grades range from mild (drooling) and moderate (GI irritation) to severe (CNS depression, tremors/ataxia, dermal burns) and fatal (seizures/collapse, hepatic necrosis/liver failure).
Primary toxic agents are citric acid and concentrated citrus essential oils, notably D-limonene (highest in peel/oils) and linalool.
Citric acid and citrus oils irritate the GI tract, skin, and respiratory passages; in large amounts the oils affect the CNS causing depression/weakness.
Cats lack the hepatic enzymes needed to efficiently metabolize these essential-oil compounds, so extreme exposure can cause hepatic necrosis / liver failure.
Dermal contact with citrus essential oils can cause irritation or chemical burns, and grooming oil off the fur can lead to systemic toxicity.
Toxic parts: stem, leaf, seed, fruit, peel; peel/leaves/stems contain the highest concentration of toxic oils (esp. D-limonene) and are more dangerous than fruit flesh.
Vomiting and diarrhea (gastrointestinal irritation).
CNS depression (lethargy, dullness, weakness).
Tremors, shaking, and ataxia (walking as if drunk).
Dermal soreness, redness, or chemical burns (rapid onset on contact).
Excessive drooling/hypersalivation (rapid onset, taste/oral irritation).
Seizures and collapse (graded fatal).
Liver failure / hepatic necrosis (graded fatal).
Routes of exposure include ingestion, dermal contact, and inhalation (citrus-based cleaning products and essential-oil diffusers).

verify.summary: Core direction is CORRECT and matches ASPCA: Citrus (Rutaceae) is toxic to cats, with peels/plant material more dangerous than fruit flesh; toxic agents are citrus essential oils (d-limonene, linalool); cats lack glucuronyl-transferase to metabolize them. No safe-vs-toxic disagreement. However the entry OVERSTATES severity and partially misattributes compounds. ASPCA lists toxic principles as 'essential oils and psoralens' (NOT citric acid) with signs 'vomiting, diarrhea, depression, potential dermatitis.' The peer-reviewed feline study (Hooser 1990), Veterian Key, and VCA document hypersalivation, tremors, ataxia, depression, hypothermia, dermal burns, and respiratory distress — but NONE list seizures or hepatic necrosis/liver failure as documented clinical signs. The 'fatal' gradings for seizures and liver failure, and the citric-acid-as-toxin framing, are blog-level extrapolations beyond authoritative support. The entry also omits psoralens, the ASPCA-named second principle. Set to NEEDS_REVIEW because several severity/compound claims are UNVERIFIABLE/overstated, though no core claim is flatly refuted and the toxic direction is right.

claim_verdicts.claim: 1. [isToxic] Citrus (Citrus spp., family Rutaceae) is toxic to cats.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists Lemon (Citrus limonia) and Orange (Citrus sinensis), family Rutaceae, as toxic to cats. Fruit edible but skins/plant material cause problems.

claim_verdicts.claim: 2. [severity] Overall 'toxic'; symptom grades mild (drooling) to moderate (GI) to severe (CNS depression, tremors/ataxia, dermal burns) to fatal (seizures/collapse, hepatic necrosis/liver failure).
claim_verdicts.note: Mild-to-severe grading (GI, drooling, CNS depression, tremors, ataxia, dermal burns) is supported by ASPCA/Hooser/Veterian Key/VCA. But the FATAL gradings — seizures and hepatic necrosis/liver failure — are not documented as clinical signs by any authoritative source; severity is overstated at the fatal tier.
claim_verdicts.authority: Hooser 1990 (Vet Clin North Am); ASPCA; VCA

claim_verdicts.claim: 3. [compound] Primary toxic agents are citric acid and concentrated citrus essential oils, notably D-limonene and linalool.
claim_verdicts.note: Essential oils (d-limonene, linalool) CONFIRMED by ASPCA, Hooser, Veterian Key. But ASPCA names the toxic principles as 'essential oils and PSORALENS' — not citric acid. Citric acid is not an authoritatively recognized citrus toxin in cats; including it (and omitting psoralens) is a misattribution.

claim_verdicts.claim: 4. [mechanism] Citric acid and citrus oils irritate the GI tract, skin, and respiratory passages; in large amounts oils cause CNS depression/weakness.
claim_verdicts.note: Citrus oils cause GI, dermal, respiratory irritation and CNS depression/weakness per VCA and Hooser. Citric acid attribution is unsupported (see claim 3), but the oil-driven mechanism is confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: 5. [mechanism] Cats lack hepatic enzymes to metabolize essential-oil compounds, so extreme exposure can cause hepatic necrosis / liver failure.
claim_verdicts.note: Enzyme deficiency (low glucuronyl-transferase) CONFIRMED by VCA and multiple sources. But the downstream claim of hepatic necrosis / liver failure is NOT documented by ASPCA, Hooser, Veterian Key, or VCA as an observed feline clinical outcome for citrus oils; it is a blog-level extrapolation.
claim_verdicts.authority: VCA (enzyme); no authority for hepatic necrosis

claim_verdicts.claim: 6. [mechanism] Dermal contact with citrus oils can cause irritation/chemical burns, and grooming oil off fur can cause systemic toxicity.
claim_verdicts.note: Veterian Key documents dermal absorption (max blood levels 10 min post-dermal) and severe cutaneous reactions; VCA notes burns/redness on skin and that cats groom and ingest oils, causing systemic toxicity.

claim_verdicts.claim: 7. [toxic_part] Toxic parts stem, leaf, seed, fruit, peel; peel/leaves/stems highest in oils (D-limonene), more dangerous than fruit flesh.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA: 'Fruit is edible, skins and plant material can cause problems.' Veterian Key: d-limonene/linalool derived from citrus fruit skin. Peel > flesh hierarchy supported. Listing fruit flesh as toxic is a slight overstatement (ASPCA calls it edible), but peel/skin/plant-part danger is confirmed.

claim_verdicts.claim: 8. [symptom] Vomiting and diarrhea (GI irritation).
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA explicitly lists vomiting and diarrhea; VCA lists vomiting.

claim_verdicts.claim: 9. [symptom] CNS depression (lethargy, dullness, weakness).
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists 'depression'; Hooser lists depression; VCA lists lethargy/weakness. However grading as 'severe' may be overstated — sources treat depression as a general/common sign, not severe-tier.

claim_verdicts.claim: 10. [symptom] Tremors, shaking, and ataxia (walking as if drunk).
claim_verdicts.note: Hooser, Veterian Key, and VCA all document muscle tremors and ataxia from d-limonene/linalool/citrus oil in cats.

claim_verdicts.claim: 11. [symptom] Dermal soreness, redness, or chemical burns (rapid onset on contact).
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA notes 'potential dermatitis'; VCA lists redness/burns on lips, gums, tongue, skin; Veterian Key notes severe cutaneous reactions.

claim_verdicts.claim: 12. [symptom] Excessive drooling/hypersalivation (rapid onset, oral irritation).
claim_verdicts.note: Hooser and Veterian Key list hypersalivation; VCA lists drooling and pawing at mouth.

claim_verdicts.claim: 13. [symptom] Seizures and collapse (graded fatal).
claim_verdicts.note: No authoritative source (ASPCA, Hooser, Veterian Key, VCA) lists seizures or collapse for citrus oil in cats. Tremors and ataxia are documented; seizures are not. The 'fatal' grading is unsupported. Documented feline deaths occurred but were not attributed to seizures.
claim_verdicts.authority: Silent across ASPCA, Hooser, Veterian Key, VCA

claim_verdicts.claim: 14. [symptom] Liver failure / hepatic necrosis (graded fatal).
claim_verdicts.note: Not listed as a clinical sign by ASPCA, Hooser, Veterian Key, or VCA. Sources confirm cats' enzyme deficiency but do NOT document hepatic necrosis/liver failure as an observed citrus-oil outcome in cats. Fatal grading is an extrapolation; treat as overstated.

claim_verdicts.claim: 15. [severity] Routes include ingestion, dermal contact, and inhalation (citrus-based cleaners and essential-oil diffusers).
claim_verdicts.note: VCA confirms 'both ingestion and skin exposure can be toxic'; Veterian Key documents dermal absorption; Pet Poison Helpline/VCA discuss diffuser/airborne essential-oil exposure for cats.
claim_verdicts.authority: VCA; Veterian Key; Pet Poison Helpline

verify.summary: Core toxicity claims for Clivia miniata are CONFIRMED by two authoritative sources. ASPCA (Clivia Lily, Clivia spp., family Amaryllidaceae) lists toxic principles as "Lycorine and other alkaloids," bulbs as "the most poisonous part," and clinical signs "Vomiting, salivation, diarrhea; large ingestions cause convulsions, low blood pressure, tremors and cardiac arrhythmias." Pet Poison Helpline (Kaffir Lily / Clivia) confirms lycorine in all parts, GI distress (vomiting, drooling, retching), and large-ingestion cardiovascular (hypotension, arrhythmia, weakness) and neurological (seizure) signs, and explicitly notes it does NOT cause kidney injury (unlike true Lilium/Hemerocallis). No safe-vs-toxic disagreement. Most symptom and mechanism claims are well-supported. The severity GRADING scheme (toxic overall; cardiac=severe, GI/neuro=moderate) is an internal editorial classification not provided by authorities and is UNVERIFIABLE as graded, though directionally consistent with the source descriptions. The mechanism claim of "strongly irritate the stomach" overstates ASPCA/PPH wording (they describe GI distress/vomiting/drooling, not specifically severe gastric irritation), but is broadly consistent. "Fire Lily" is a colloquial common name; authorities use Clivia/Kaffir Lily, but scientific name Clivia miniata matches unambiguously. Overall PASS: core isToxic and compound/mechanism are confirmed by authorities with no safe-toxic miss.

Note: 'Fire Lily' is a colloquial name; authorities use 'Clivia Lily'/'Kaffir Lily' but the scientific name Clivia miniata matches.

claim_verdicts.note: Overall 'toxic' is confirmed. The per-cluster severity GRADING (cardiac=severe, GI/neuro=moderate) is an internal editorial scheme; neither ASPCA nor PPH assigns graded severity tiers. Directionally consistent (cardiac/neuro signs described as occurring only with large ingestions; PPH notes life-threatening toxicosis is extremely rare), but not stated as graded by an authority.

Theobromine acts as a diuretic, increasing fluid loss and urine output, potentially causing dehydration.
(zh-TW only, NOT in EN) Methylxanthines block adenosine receptors, inhibit phosphodiesterase, and interfere with calcium signaling in cardiac and skeletal muscle.

verify.summary: Cocoa toxicity claims are well-supported by authoritative veterinary sources (Merck Veterinary Manual, Pet Poison Helpline, ASPCA APCC). Cocoa/chocolate is toxic to cats via methylxanthines (theobromine + caffeine); cats are explicitly listed as a susceptible species. Merck gives cocoa powder methylxanthine content as 28.5 mg/g (claim 9's ~30 mg/g is a fair approximation) and confirms it is far more concentrated than finished chocolate (12x milk chocolate). All mechanism claims (adenosine receptor blockade, phosphodiesterase inhibition, calcium signaling interference, catecholamine/cardiovascular/CNS stimulation, diuresis) are confirmed by Merck. The full symptom set (GI upset, polydipsia/polyuria, tremors/seizures/coma, tachycardia/arrhythmia/cardiac arrest, tachypnea/cyanosis/respiratory failure, hyperthermia) matches Merck's clinical description, and onset within 6-12 hours is confirmed; severe outcomes (death from arrhythmia, hyperthermia, respiratory failure) justify 'fatal' severity gradings. Cocoa bean hull mulch is independently confirmed as a hazardous exposure source (~9 mg/g methylxanthines). The slower-than-human metabolism claim is supported: human theobromine half-life ~6-10h vs dog ~17.5h, with cats having limited methylxanthine-metabolizing capacity (feline-specific half-life not formally published, but slow metabolism / accumulation risk is the consensus). Minor caveats: claim 13's 'potential internal bleeding' is not a documented chocolate-toxicosis sign in the authoritative sources (Merck lists cardiac arrhythmia/arrest, not hemorrhage) — flagged as unverifiable. Claim 11's GI-window onset of 2-12h for PU/PD is slightly broader than Merck's 6-12h general onset but within reasonable range. No safe-vs-toxic disagreement; core toxicity, compound, and mechanism claims all CONFIRMED.

verify.summary: Core toxicity is CONFIRMED: both Pet Poison Helpline and the ASPCA list Croton (Codiaeum variegatum) as toxic to cats, and the diterpene/phorbol-ester chemical-irritant mechanism is well supported by clinical sources (HK Hospital Authority toxic plant DB cites 5-deoxyingenol, a diterpene ester). No safe-vs-toxic disagreement. However, two material problems prevent a PASS. (1) SEVERITY OVERSTATED: the entry grades 'cautious', but Pet Poison Helpline — the most specific authoritative source — explicitly rates Croton 'Mild', and the HK clinical case described only 'slight irritation of the oral cavity'. (2) FABRICATED/UNVERIFIABLE COMPOUND: the claim that the SEEDS contain protein-based toxins is not supported by any authoritative source for Codiaeum variegatum; protein/lectin seed toxins belong to OTHER plants (Croton tiglium seed proteins; ricin in Ricinus communis). Authoritative sources attribute Codiaeum toxicity to diterpene/phorbol esters only, and do not single out seeds as a toxic part. The entry's toxicParts list 'Sap, Leaf, Entire Plant' (not seeds), so the description's seed-toxin language is internally inconsistent and unsupported. Also note: ASPCA/Pet Poison Helpline do not explicitly enumerate eye irritation; that and lethargy are extrapolations. Symptoms drooling/vomiting/diarrhea/oral irritation/skin dermatitis/anorexia are well supported.

Caffeine blocks cellular/CNS adenosine receptors (which normally reduce neural activity and heart rate), causing central nervous system overstimulation.
Caffeine increases intracellular calcium, enhancing cardiac muscle contraction strength and frequency, leading to tachycardia, hypertension, and ultimately cardiac arrest.
Caffeine acts as a diuretic, increasing urinary fluid loss, driving thirst and risking dehydration.

Increased thirst and urination (Renal), onset ~2-4 hours; graded moderate.

Cardiovascular dysfunction: rapid irregular heartbeat, high blood pressure, cardiac arrest (Cardiac), onset 2-12 hours; graded fatal.
Respiratory distress: panting, rapid breathing progressing to respiratory failure (Respiratory), onset 6-12 hours; graded fatal.
Hyperthermia: core temperature spike from overstimulation/tremors (Neurological), onset 6-12 hours; graded severe.

Onset of symptoms can begin within 30-60 minutes of ingestion.

verify.summary: Attempted to disprove the coffee/caffeine toxicity claims but authoritative veterinary sources strongly corroborate the core science. Pet Poison Helpline and VCA both classify caffeine as toxic to cats (cats more sensitive than humans), name caffeine (a methylxanthine, sister to theobromine) as the compound, and list GI upset, increased urination, tachycardia/arrhythmia/hypertension, tremors, seizures, hyperactivity, and panting. The MSD/Merck Veterinary Manual chapter on methylxanthine toxicosis confirms the detailed mechanism nearly verbatim: competitive adenosine-receptor antagonism causing CNS stimulation, diuresis, and tachycardia; increased intracellular calcium via cellular entry plus inhibited sarcoplasmic-reticulum sequestration enhancing cardiac/skeletal muscle contractility; and death due to cardiac arrhythmias, hyperthermia, or respiratory failure. No safe-vs-toxic disagreement. Two minor caveats, neither falsifying a core claim: (1) onset timing is split across sources — Pet Poison Helpline/VCA cite 1-2 hours, MSD cites 6-12 hours; the entry's per-symptom windows (2-4h, 2-12h, 6-12h) and the 30-60 min early-onset claim are broadly consistent but the early end is not explicitly authority-backed. (2) The toxic_part field listing 'stem' is odd phrasing for a processed beverage/ground product, but the substantive sources (brewed coffee, espresso, grounds, instant powder, coffee-flavored foods) are all confirmed caffeine sources. Core compound and mechanism CONFIRMED, so overall PASS.

verify.summary: Autumn Crocus (Colchicum autumnale) is confirmed TOXIC to cats by both ASPCA and Pet Poison Helpline; the entry's core toxicity, compound (colchicine + other alkaloids), and the headline systemic signs (bloody GI, shock, multi-organ damage, bone marrow suppression, liver/kidney damage, death) all match authoritative sources. No safe↔toxic disagreement. The microtubule mechanism is correct standard pharmacology (peer-reviewed/clinical) though not stated in the ASPCA/PPH database entries. Several granular symptom claims (specific 2–12h onset window, respiratory failure as a 'common' cause of death, seizures) are supported by secondary clinical sources but NOT directly by the top-tier ASPCA/PPH entries — graded UNVERIFIABLE against the priority authorities rather than refuted, since they are clinically plausible and corroborated in lower-tier veterinary writing. claim_verdicts.claim: Colchicine halts cell division by preventing microtubule formation, targeting fastest-dividing cells (gut lining, bone marrow, kidneys).
claim_verdicts.note: Standard, well-established pharmacology: colchicine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization, with predilection for rapidly dividing tissue (GI, bone marrow). Not stated on ASPCA/PPH database entries but corroborated by clinical/peer-reviewed literature; ASPCA-listed signs (bone marrow suppression, multi-organ damage) are consistent. The specific singling-out of kidneys as a 'fastest-dividing' target is a minor imprecision (renal injury is more accumulation/multi-organ than mitotic), but the core mechanism is correct.

claim_verdicts.claim: [isToxic] Convallaria majalis (Lily of the Valley) is toxic to cats
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA explicitly classifies it 'Toxic to Dogs, Toxic to Cats, Toxic to Horses.' Pet Poison Helpline concurs.

claim_verdicts.claim: [severity] Severity is toxic/potentially fatal; cardiac symptom graded fatal
claim_verdicts.note: PPH cites severe signs including changes in heart rate/rhythm, weakness, seizures; cardenolides are digitalis-like cardiotoxins that can be life-threatening. Death is well documented in clinical literature. Grading the cardiac symptom as potentially fatal is appropriate.

claim_verdicts.claim: [compound] Contains cardiac glycosides, specifically convallatoxin, convalloside, and 30+ related cardiac glycosides; highest concentration in flowers and berries
claim_verdicts.authority: Peer-reviewed review (Bioactive Compounds in Health and Disease) / ScienceDirect
claim_verdicts.note: Convallatoxin, convalloside and 30+ (literature cites up to 38) cardiac glycosides are CONFIRMED. However the 'highest concentration in flowers and berries' sub-claim is NOT supported: glycosides are distributed throughout the whole plant and several sources place the highest concentration in the bulb/rhizome, not flowers/berries. ASPCA/PPH list the principle only as 'cardenolides (convallarin and others)' — they do not name convallatoxin/convalloside. Claim REFUTED on the concentration localization error.

claim_verdicts.claim: [compound] Also contains irritant saponins distributed throughout the plant
claim_verdicts.note: Phytochemistry sources confirm saponins are present, but steroid saponins predominate in rhizomes/roots rather than being uniformly distributed, and they are not the primary clinical toxic principle. Neither ASPCA nor Pet Poison Helpline lists saponins. Not confirmed by an authoritative veterinary-toxicology source for cats.

claim_verdicts.claim: [mechanism] Cardiac glycosides inhibit Na+/K+-ATPase in heart muscle, disrupting electrical conduction and causing severe arrhythmias
claim_verdicts.note: Well-established mechanism: cardiac glycosides inhibit Na+/K+-ATPase, raising intracellular Na+ then Ca2+, increasing automaticity/ectopy and impairing AV conduction, producing arrhythmias. Convallatoxin specifically is a potent Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitor. Confirmed for the glycoside class, not specifically validated in cats by ASPCA/PPH.

claim_verdicts.claim: [mechanism] Unlike true lilies, it does NOT cause kidney failure
claim_verdicts.note: Lily of the Valley is not a true lily (Lilium/Hemerocallis) and its toxicity is cardiac, not nephrotoxic. ASPCA/PPH list cardiac and GI/neurologic signs with no renal failure; nephrotoxicity is specific to true lilies. Distinction is correct, though stated as an absence rather than a positive authoritative statement.

claim_verdicts.claim: [mechanism] In acute cases can lead to hyperkalemia (dangerously high potassium)
claim_verdicts.authority: Peer-reviewed human/clinical toxicology (PMC, Cal Poison Control)
claim_verdicts.note: Hyperkalemia is a recognized consequence of acute cardiac glycoside (digoxin) poisoning in humans and correlates with mortality. Plausible by mechanism for any glycoside, but NOT documented specifically for Convallaria ingestion in cats by ASPCA, PPH, Merck or VCA. Extrapolation, not confirmed for this entry/species.

claim_verdicts.claim: [toxic_part] Every part is toxic — flowers, leaves, roots, and berries; vase water from cut flowers is also poisonous
claim_verdicts.note: 'All parts toxic (leaves, stems, flowers, roots, berries)' is supported by phytochemistry literature. The 'vase water is poisonous' sub-claim is by analogy to true lilies and is NOT documented by an authoritative source for Convallaria; treat as unverified. Authoritative vet-tox sources (ASPCA/PPH) do not specify plant parts at all.

claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists vomiting; PPH lists vomiting and GI distress.

claim_verdicts.note: Neither ASPCA nor PPH lists diarrhea for this plant (they list vomiting/GI distress/loss of appetite). 'Bloody diarrhea' specifically is not documented by any authoritative source; appears overstated/possibly fabricated for cats.

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Abdominal pain/discomfort

claim_verdicts.note: Not listed by ASPCA or PPH for Lily of the Valley. Not confirmed.

claim_verdicts.authority: ASPCA (irregular/altered heart beat) + peer-reviewed glycoside toxicology
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists 'irregular heart beat'; PPH lists 'changes in heart rate and rhythm.' Bradycardia is a hallmark of cardiac glycoside toxicity (vagal tone + AV conduction block) and is well supported by clinical pharmacology.

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Hypotension
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA explicitly lists 'low blood pressure.'

claim_verdicts.claim: [symptom] Severe cardiac arrhythmias including AV (atrioventricular) block
claim_verdicts.authority: ASPCA (irregular heart beat) + peer-reviewed glycoside toxicology
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists irregular heartbeat; PPH lists changes in rhythm. AV block is a classic, documented arrhythmia of cardiac glycoside poisoning (impaired AV nodal conduction). Arrhythmias confirmed; AV block supported by mechanism/clinical literature.

claim_verdicts.note: PPH explicitly lists 'weakness' among severe signs. Collapse follows from hypotension/arrhythmia.

claim_verdicts.note: Both ASPCA and PPH explicitly list seizures. Trembling is not separately listed by authorities but seizures are firmly confirmed; verdict reflects the seizure component.

verify.summary: Core toxicity is solidly CONFIRMED: ASPCA classifies Convallaria majalis as toxic to cats (toxic principle 'cardenolides — convallarin and others') and Pet Poison Helpline confirms cardiac/GI/neurologic toxicity. There is NO safe-vs-toxic disagreement. The compound family (cardiac glycosides incl. convallatoxin, convalloside, 30+ glycosides) and the Na+/K+-ATPase mechanism are confirmed by peer-reviewed literature, and key cardiac signs (irregular heartbeat/arrhythmia, hypotension, bradycardia, AV block), vomiting, weakness, and seizures are all backed by ASPCA/PPH or clinical pharmacology. The 'not a true lily, no kidney failure' distinction is correct. However several claims are REFUTED or UNVERIFIABLE and warrant editing: (1) REFUTED — 'highest concentration in flowers and berries' is wrong; glycosides are distributed throughout and often highest in the bulb/rhizome (this is why I flagged claim 3). (2) UNVERIFIABLE for cats — bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and hypersalivation/drooling are NOT listed by ASPCA or PPH (drooling and bloody diarrhea look added/overstated). (3) UNVERIFIABLE — hyperkalemia (human-digoxin extrapolation, not documented for Convallaria in cats), 'vase water is poisonous' (analogy to true lilies, undocumented for this plant), and irritant saponins distribution (phytochemistry only; steroid saponins concentrate in rhizomes/roots, not named by vet authorities). overall_factual=NEEDS_REVIEW: core toxicity passes and no safe/toxic miss, but the flower/berry concentration claim is factually wrong and multiple symptom/mechanism claims lack authoritative backing for cats and should be softened or sourced before publishing.

claim_verdicts.claim: 3. [toxic_part] The corn cob is the primary danger (toxicParts = 'Cob').

claim_verdicts.claim: 4. [mechanism] The cob is fibrous/indigestible; can lodge in throat or intestine causing GI obstruction requiring emergency surgery and can be fatal.

claim_verdicts.claim: 5. [mechanism] Seasonings — garlic and onion powder — are highly toxic to cats via Allium toxicity; excessive salt and butter cause GI distress.

verify.summary: Core toxicology of the "Corn Cob" entry is sound and authority-backed, so there is NO safe↔toxic disagreement. Corn kernels are correctly called non-toxic (ASPCA), and the cob is correctly flagged as the real danger — an indigestible foreign body causing GI obstruction that can require surgery and be fatal (Merck Vet Manual; ASPCA cob case). The Allium/garlic-onion seasoning toxicity (Merck) and the aflatoxin/Aspergillus flavus+parasiticus mechanism with poor prognosis (FDA, Pet Poison Helpline) are all confirmed. Verdict is NEEDS_REVIEW, not PASS, for two reasons: (1) Internal severity inconsistency — top-level 'cautious' coexists with two per-symptom 'fatal' gradings (claim 11), which is defensible only if the app intends 'cautious' to mean "kernels fine, but specific scenarios are lethal"; this should be reconciled. However") with body_system "Metabolic"/severity "moderate". This garbled, non-symptom record must be deleted. Also note the aflatoxin/moldy-corn hazard, while factually correct, is a low-relevance scenario for indoor cats and is mechanistically unrelated to the cob — its prominence in a "Corn Cob" entry is a scope stretch. Same artifact and per-symptom data should be checked in data/foods/corn_on_the_cob.json and the zh-TW caches.

verify.summary: Spring crocus (Crocus vernus / Crocus spp.) IS toxic to cats and authorities (ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline) confirm it causes only MILD, self-limiting GI upset (vomiting, diarrhea, drooling) — the "toxic but much less dangerous than autumn crocus" framing is correct (claims 1, 5, 6, 7, 8 CONFIRMED; no safe/toxic disagreement). The FATAL defect is the compound/mechanism: spring crocus is in family Iridaceae and does NOT contain colchicine. Colchicine is exclusive to Autumn Crocus (Colchicum autumnale, Colchicaceae/Liliaceae). The entry's claim that spring crocus "contains colchicine and other alkaloids" (claim 2) is REFUTED by authorities — wrong compound assigned to this species. Because a core compound claim is REFUTED, overall_factual = FAIL. Secondary content-integrity problem: the entry is named "Crocus" / scientificName "Crocus vernus" yet its symptom table embeds Autumn Crocus's fatal/severe systemic effects (hepatic necrosis, kidney failure/anuria, bone marrow suppression, respiratory failure, seizures/shock) as if they belong to this species — these are UNVERIFIABLE/misattributed for Crocus vernus itself. Also note claim 18 misstates the file: the actual EN severity field is "toxic", not "cautious".

claim_verdicts.claim: 1. Spring crocus (Crocus vernus) is toxic to cats but far less dangerous than autumn crocus.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA: spring crocus 'may cause gastrointestinal upset like vomiting, diarrhea and drooling'; autumn crocus is 'much more severe' (organ damage, bone marrow). Pet Poison Helpline concurs spring is the milder common form. Toxic-but-less-dangerous framing is supported.

claim_verdicts.claim: 2. Spring crocus contains small amounts of colchicine and other alkaloids.
claim_verdicts.note: CORE COMPOUND ERROR. Spring crocus (Crocus spp.) is family Iridaceae and is NOT a colchicine source; colchicine is found in Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus). ASPCA/Pet Poison Helpline attribute colchicine only to autumn crocus and describe spring crocus toxicity purely as GI upset, never citing colchicine. No authority states spring crocus contains colchicine.

claim_verdicts.claim: 3. Spring crocus contains much lower colchicine levels than autumn crocus.
claim_verdicts.note: Premise is false: spring crocus is not a colchicine-containing plant at all (Iridaceae), so 'much lower colchicine' mischaracterizes it as a lesser colchicine source rather than a non-source. Authorities never quantify or assign colchicine to spring crocus.

claim_verdicts.claim: 4. Colchicine interferes with cell division (stops cells dividing), impacting rapidly dividing tissues such as bone marrow.
claim_verdicts.note: Mechanism is biochemically correct: colchicine binds tubulin, inhibits microtubule polymerization, arrests mitosis at metaphase, and disproportionately affects rapidly dividing cells including bone marrow. HOWEVER this mechanism applies to AUTUMN crocus, not spring crocus — accurate as chemistry but misattributed to Crocus vernus in this entry.

factual_claims.claim: Cycads (Cycas spp. / Zamia spp., incl. sago palm Cycas revoluta) are toxic to cats.
Severity graded 'toxic'; among the most liver-toxic plants in veterinary medicine, often fatal even with aggressive treatment.
Primary toxin is cycasin (a methylazoxymethanol glycoside).
Also contains the neurotoxic amino acid beta-methylamino-L-alanine (BMAA).
Gut bacteria metabolize cycasin into a compound that causes hepatic necrosis (liver cell death).
BMAA causes central nervous system effects (tremors to paralysis/coma).
Liver failure impairs clotting-factor production, causing coagulopathy and spontaneous bleeding.
All parts are toxic — leaves, stems, bark, roots, and seeds.
Seeds contain the highest cycasin levels; one or two seeds can be fatal.
Vomiting and diarrhea (often bloody / melena), abdominal pain — onset 15 min to 4 h.
Acute liver failure with jaundice/icterus, ascites, increased thirst — onset 48–72 h.
Neurological signs: seizures, tremors, ataxia, progressing to paralysis/coma.
Coagulopathy: petechiae/ecchymosis, nosebleeds, bloody stool (secondary to liver failure).
Lethargy/depression with early onset, worsening over time.
Liver failure develops within 24–72 hours of ingestion.

verify.summary: Cycad / sago palm (Cycas revoluta and Zamia spp.) entry. All core toxicity claims are CONFIRMED by authoritative sources: ASPCA and Pet Poison Helpline both list it as toxic to cats with cycasin as the primary hepatotoxin, and the dvm360 toxicology brief plus ASPCA confirm BMAA as the neurotoxic component. The mechanism (cycasin metabolized to a hepatotoxic compound -> hepatic necrosis/liver failure; BMAA -> CNS effects), the toxic-parts claim (all parts toxic, seeds highest concentration, 1-2 seeds potentially fatal), the symptom set (GI signs incl. melena, jaundice, coagulopathy/bruising, neurologic signs incl. seizures, lethargy), and the high severity (50-75% mortality, life-threatening) all match authoritative sources. ONE non-safety error: the plant family is stated as 'Zamiaceae', but the lead genus Cycas (sago palm, the named alias) belongs to family CYCADACEAE per ASPCA and standard botanical taxonomy; only Zamia is in Zamiaceae. This is a botanical metadata error, not a toxicity error, so it does not create a safe<->toxic disagreement and does not change overall_factual. Recommend correcting family to 'Cycadaceae' (or 'Cycadaceae / Zamiaceae' given the combined scientificName).

factual_claims.claim: Dieffenbachia spp. (Dumb Cane) is toxic to cats.
Toxic parts: sap, stem, leaf, and the entire plant.
Active toxins are insoluble calcium oxalate crystals (raphides) packed inside specialised idioblast cells in leaves and stems.
Proteolytic enzymes are also present and amplify the inflammatory reaction.
When chewed, the needle-like raphides are forcefully ejected into the oral mucosa, mechanically penetrating mouth/throat lining and causing immediate intense pain, burning, and inflammation.
Intense burning, irritation and inflammation of the mouth, tongue, lips and throat (immediate onset).
Excessive drooling / ptyalism (hypersalivation).
Difficulty breathing (dyspnea) with swelling/edema of tongue and throat; glottal/pharyngeal edema can obstruct the airway.
Vomiting, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), and anorexia (loss of appetite); diarrhea possible but less common.
Pawing at the mouth / head shaking in response to oral irritant.
Top-level severity graded 'cautious', while individual symptoms are graded severe (oral inflammation, airway obstruction) and moderate (drooling, GI distress); death is described as infrequent.

The added severe-case airway swelling/dyspnea is clinically well documented and appropriately gated as a severe/infrequent outcome; severity grade "cautious" matches the generally mild-to-moderate, rarely-fatal real profile. claim_verdicts.claim: Toxic compound is steroidal saponins.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA names the toxic principle as 'Saponins'; Pet Poison Helpline confirms saponins in leaves and stems. Peer-reviewed phytochemistry (PMC) confirms the saponins in D. marginata are specifically steroidal (furostanol) saponins, so the entry's 'steroidal saponins' is the correct, more specific class.

claim_verdicts.claim: Mechanism: membrane disruption causing GI irritation; neurological effects possible at higher doses.
claim_verdicts.note: Saponins' recognized action is cell-membrane disruption, and veterinary sources attribute the effect to irritation of the GI mucosa. Neurological signs (dilated pupils, wobbly gait/ataxia) are documented specifically in cats by ASPCA and Pet Poison Helpline. The 'at higher doses' qualifier is reasonable; exact mechanism is described in literature as not fully understood, but the stated mechanism is consistent with authorities.

Core claims are CONFIRMED: ASPCA lists eucalyptus as toxic to cats with toxic principle 'Essential oils: eucalyptol' (= 1,8-cineole), family Myrtaceae, and clinical signs salivation/vomiting/diarrhea/depression/weakness — all matching. Pet Poison Helpline confirms the mechanism (feline liver lacks glucuronyl transferase to metabolize phenols/monoterpenes), plus tremors, ataxia, respiratory distress, and liver failure, and that the concentrated essential oil is the primary hazard via oral, dermal, and inhalation routes. Two minor symptom claims are UNVERIFIABLE as specifically worded rather than refuted: 'seizures' (authorities name tremors/ataxia/neurologic abnormalities but not seizures by name) and 'skin redness/soreness' (dermal exposure is a confirmed route but a discrete redness sign is not enumerated). Neither undermines the core toxicity grading. Severity grading (toxic, with severe outcomes from concentrated oil) is appropriate and not overstated. Verdict: PASS.

verify.summary: Garlic (Allium sativum) entry is correctly marked toxic to cats, matching ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline, and Merck Vet Manual. Core claims CONFIRMED: toxic compound n-propyl disulfide (ASPCA names it exactly), mechanism of oxidative RBC/hemoglobin damage producing Heinz bodies and hemolytic anemia, the hallmark delayed onset (a few days / 3-5 days), and the symptom set (vomiting/diarrhea, lethargy/weakness, pale gums, jaundice/icterus, tachypnea/dyspnea, tachycardia, hemoglobinuria/dark urine). The "more dangerous than onion by weight / ~3-5x" claim is CONFIRMED (Pet Poison Helpline cites ~5x). No safe<->toxic disagreement and no core compound/mechanism is refuted, so overall_factual=PASS. However several secondary/embellished claims are NOT supported by authoritative sources and should be flagged for editing: (1) the cardiovascular profile attributing hypotension/vasodilation to allicin and ajoene acting as "cardiac and smooth muscle relaxants" -- Merck/ASPCA attribute tachycardia to compensatory anemia response, NOT a primary pharmacologic vasodilator effect; this reads as cross-contamination from human herbal-supplement pharmacology. (2) "Cold Sensitivity" as a symptom -- absent from all authoritative sources, likely fabricated. (3) "Garlic Breath" listed as a clinical symptom -- not in ASPCA/Merck/PPH. (4) The detailed "direct painful damage to gastric and ileal mucosa from unaged garlic preparations" mechanism is more specific than authoritative sources support. (5) Compound list also names allicin and allyl disulfides; ASPCA names only n-propyl disulfide as the toxic principle (allicin is the precursor that breaks down to it) -- defensible but allicin is not itself the named toxic principle. Minor: family is listed as "Allioideae" while ASPCA lists "Liliaceae"; Allioideae (subfamily of Amaryllidaceae) is the current botanical placement, so acceptable. Symptom severity gradings are mostly reasonable, though tagging Tachypnea/Dyspnea as "fatal" severity overstates a single sign (death is an endpoint of untreated anemia, not of dyspnea per se).

verify.summary: Core toxicity claims are CONFIRMED: ASPCA lists the tomato plant (Solanaceae) as Toxic to Cats with toxic principle Solanine; green parts and unripe fruit are the danger and ripe fruit is non-toxic — exactly what the entry states. The basic symptom set (hypersalivation/drooling, severe GI upset/vomiting/diarrhea, depression/lethargy, weakness, dilated pupils, slow heart rate/bradycardia) matches the ASPCA cat clinical-signs list. The entry is NOT a safe/toxic miss. However, it suffers from severe symptom over-escalation: three symptoms are graded "fatal" — Neurological Deficits and Paralysis, Cardiovascular collapse, and Hemolysis and Acute Kidney Injury. None of these appear on the ASPCA cat clinical-signs list, and Pet Poison Helpline states pet death from tomato poisoning is "extremely unlikely and basically unheard of." The hemolysis + free-hemoglobin → acute renal failure narrative is not an authoritative tomato/cat profile; it mirrors the lily-toxicity (AKI) and onion-toxicity (hemolysis) pictures — a probable cross-contamination/fabrication. Overall severity "toxic" is correct, but the per-symptom "fatal" gradings overstate real-world feline risk and the hemolysis/AKI/paralysis symptoms are unsupported by authoritative sources. The first "symptom" object is also malformed (its name field "Green tomatoes, as well as the leaves and stems of the tomato plant" is a toxic-part description, not a symptom). NEEDS_REVIEW: core claims confirmed, but multiple symptom/severity claims unverifiable/overstated and need editorial correction.

verify.summary: The entry grades Gum as "toxic" (severity: toxic) and its safetyNotes + symptoms attribute this to xylitol causing "severe hypoglycaemia" and "liver failure" in cats via insulin-independent insulin secretion. This mechanism is REFUTED for cats by authoritative sources. ASPCA states plainly that "people, cats and ferrets are not negatively affected by xylitol"; the FDA echoes that xylitol does not appear dangerous to cats; and the 2018 peer-reviewed study (Jerzsele et al., J Vet Pharmacol Ther) found cats tolerated doses up to 1,000 mg/kg with no hypoglycemia, no insulin surge, and no liver damage — only transient salivation. The entry's OWN notes admit this ("cats do not react to xylitol with the dangerous insulin surge seen in dogs"; "in a 2018 experimental study... the cats exhibited no changes in blood glucose, liver enzymes... transient salivation being the only reported clinical [sign]"), yet it still assigns severity=toxic and lists a "fatal" hypoglycemia/liver-failure symptom. This is a false-alarm safe<->toxic disagreement: the named chemical mechanism is non-toxic to cats. The only legitimate cat hazard is MECHANICAL — choking / GI foreign-body obstruction from swallowed gum mass — which is a real but distinct risk, not chemical xylitol poisoning. Severity is grossly overstated for the chemical pathway. Additional quality defects: the first "symptom" entry is a truncated, mid-sentence fragment ("Unlike dogs, who suffer severe and life-threatening reactions to chewing gum containing the artificial sweetener xylitol") and is not a symptom at all; the "Hypoglycemia and Liver Failure" symptom is self-labeled "(Theoretical / Rare)" yet graded "fatal," contradicting the toxic severity grade. scientificName="Gum" and family="Various" are placeholder/non-meaningful for a food item. overall_factual=FAIL because the core compound mechanism (xylitol hypoglycemia/hepatotoxicity in cats) is REFUTED and there is a safe<->toxic disagreement.

verify.summary: English Ivy (hedera_spp) is solidly accurate on all core claims. ASPCA confirms verbatim: Hedera helix, family Araliaceae, toxic to cats, toxic principle 'triterpenoid saponins (hederagenin)', GI clinical signs (vomiting, abdominal pain, hypersalivation, diarrhea), and 'foliage more toxic than berries' (matching toxicParts Leaf+Fruit with leaf as primary). verify.summary:
Helleborus niger / Christmas Rose entry is broadly accurate. Core claims are CONFIRMED by ASPCA and Pet Poison Helpline: the plant is toxic to cats (Ranunculaceae), whole-plant toxicity, cardiac glycoside (bufadienolide) compound class plus irritant sap, mechanism (Na+/K+ ATPase inhibition -> arrhythmia + GI irritation via protoanemonin), and the GI + cardiac symptom set.
